arguments.heading: What happened at the argument
paragraphs: Aaron Streett argued for CC/Devas. He stated arbitration awards are worthless without court enforcement. He claimed Congress added the FSIA exception to allow such enforcement.
Ms. Harris argued for CC/Devas. She stated the case should begin and end with FSIA text. She claimed Section 1330(b) omits minimum contacts requirements.
Mr. Phillips argued for Antrix. He described the context of the arbitration agreement. He noted both corporations were incorporated in India.
Mr. McGill argued for Antrix. He claimed the Ninth Circuit construction was unfaithful to text. He argued Congress provided jurisdiction where immunity exceptions exist.

sections.heading: What this case is about
paragraphs: CC/Devas Ltd. seeks to enforce an arbitration award against Antrix Corp. Antrix argues the FSIA requires minimum contacts. The Ninth Circuit agreed with Antrix. CC/Devas argues the statute omits this requirement.

sections.heading: What each side wants
paragraphs: CC/Devas wants the Court to reverse the Ninth Circuit. It seeks to enforce the arbitration award without minimum contacts.
Antrix wants the Court to affirm the Ninth Circuit. It seeks to deny enforcement due to lack of minimum contacts.

sections.heading: What each side says
paragraphs: CC/Devas argues the FSIA text omits minimum contacts. It claims Congress intended to allow enforcement of New York Convention awards.
Antrix argues the FSIA requires minimum contacts. It claims the arbitration exception does not override this jurisdictional requirement.

sections.heading: Why it matters
paragraphs: This case determines whether foreign states can block arbitration enforcement in U.S. courts. It affects the global enforceability of commercial arbitration awards. It clarifies the scope of sovereign immunity exceptions.
